_comment: HeteroServe single-node characterisation sweep for the Jetson Nano.
Each case becomes one llama-bench invocation, wrapped in its own power
window, so every throughput number has joules attached to it.
ONE WINDOW = ONE PHASE = ONE BENCH ROW. A case may set n_prompt (prefill)
or n_gen (decode), never both -- expand() refuses a case with both, by
name, at --dry-run time. That is audit finding #3: a -p 512 -n 128
invocation is TWO llama-bench tests sharing ONE power window, so its row
paired decode throughput with prefill+decode energy.
For a deliberately fused request use 'pg': [n_prompt, n_gen], which emits
-pg and builds a SINGLE test instance -- one row, phase 'combined'. It
reports joules_per_request, never joules_per_token.
'group' pairs the two halves of a split case. Runs inside a group are
INTERLEAVED (prefill, decode, prefill, decode ...) so the two phases of one
configuration are measured at nearly the same board temperature -- on a
fanless Nano, case order is confounded with thermal drift.
Interleaving protects a PAIR; it does not stop the board ratcheting upward
across the whole sweep. cooldown_target_c (how many degrees above the idle
baseline a case must cool back to, with cooldown_s as the floor and
max_cooldown_s as the cap) and the drift-control repeat of case 1 as the
final run are what address that.
Why these axes:
n_prompt sweeps prefill (compute-bound) at several context depths;
n_gen sweeps decode (memory-bandwidth-bound). Separating them is the
whole point of the study -- a single combined number hides the fact
that the two phases want different hardware.
n_gpu_layers 0 vs 99 gives the same-device CPU-vs-GPU comparison, which
is what actually tells you whether the Maxwell GPU is worth its watts.
Repetitions are 3 by default; raise for the numbers that go in a table.
Edit freely. 'enabled': false skips a case without deleting it.

cases.note: Prefill on 4x Cortex-A57 only. The Nano's CPU baseline.
Prefill fully offloaded to the 128-core Maxwell GPU (sm_53, FP16).
Decode on GPU. Expect a much smaller win than prefill shows -- decode is bandwidth-bound and the GPU shares the same LPDDR4.
The placement question in miniature: how many layers should live on the GPU when RAM is shared with the CPU? Prefill half of the split pair.
The placement question in miniature: how many layers should live on the GPU when RAM is shared with the CPU? Decode half of the split pair.
Q4_K_M vs Q8_0 on the same weights. Maxwell has no useful INT8 path, so K-quant dequantisation cost is a real term here. Prefill half of the split pair.
Q4_K_M vs Q8_0 on the same weights. Maxwell has no useful INT8 path, so K-quant dequantisation cost is a real term here. Decode half of the split pair.
Does the 4th core help or just add heat? Relevant because the RPC server competes with it.

One realistic single-turn request, prefill and decode fused, as llama-bench -pg builds it. Reported as joules_per_request and latency -- deliberately NOT per token, because a fused window cannot attribute tokens to a phase. The per-phase cases above are where energy per token comes from.

Enable once you have confirmed it fits. On 4 GB shared this is where the Nano starts swapping -- which is itself a finding worth recording, with swap_peak_mb from the power CSV as evidence. Prefill half of the split pair.
